source.title: Data Valuation and Selection in a Federated Model Marketplace
source.authors: Wenqian Li; You-Jia Yang; Ruoxi Jia; Yan Pang

record.tranche_reason: Applies a neural-scaling-law projection to federated learning on image datasets, a different training setting from language-model pretraining, and reports a prediction result.
record.gate_note: The paper reports a projection of validation accuracy from smaller to larger data budgets, which is relevant to V5. The performance-estimator results (including r² = 0.97 for training data and r² = 0.74 for testing data) do not test the scaling-law projection itself. The data-selection outcomes and the Wasserstein-distance comparisons likewise do not test the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study uses a log-of-data-size projection (Eq. 8, taken from Kang et al.) as one part of its own data-selection pipeline. It reports only how well that pipeline predicts federated validation accuracy. It does not fit or check a power-law form, and it does not measure loss. The extrapolation runs from 4K/8K to 15K samples, under one order of magnitude. So no version is tested: the 0.88 correlation is the method's own performance, not evidence on scaling-law form or extrapolation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that their framework selects data mixtures from multiple private sources and estimates federated model performance using a combined Wasserstein distance and neural scaling laws, without full-scale training. They add that Wasserstein approximation error can make the optimal mixing ratio fluctuate, so more robust estimation is needed.
record.recipe_differences: Uses the paper's data-budget performance projection in federated learning, with validation accuracy and Wasserstein-based performance estimation, rather than measuring language-model loss over parameter, token, or compute scales.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper says the usefulness of the combined Wasserstein distance as a performance signal depends on the FL aggregation algorithm and convergence; FedProx shows a stronger relationship than FedAvg in the reported experiments. This is separate from the accuracy-projection result.

fits_no_version.finding: A log-data-size projection from trial runs at 4K and 8K samples predicts federated validation accuracy at 15K, with correlation of about 0.88 on CIFAR10 and MNIST.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling-law-style projections of accuracy from small data budgets can rank or predict federated-learning model performance at modestly larger budgets.

record.problems: The relevant projection evidence is limited to two image datasets and the stated 4K, 8K, and 15K data budgets. It reports accuracy correlations rather than loss values or fitted scaling exponents, and gives no uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: Performance-estimator comparisons in Section 5.2 and Appendix D, data-selection accuracy results in Figure 6, and Wasserstein-distance comparisons in Table 2 were left out because they do not report outcomes of the scaling-law projection relevant to the listed versions.

untested.parts: No language-model loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
No power-law fit extrapolated over orders of magnitude; the projection spans 4K to 15K samples.
No power-law form is fitted or checked in federated image classification. Eq. 8 is assumed from prior work and used as a tool.
No downstream performance versus pretraining scale or loss.
No comparison of exponents or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T3' with a V5 'supports' label is overturned. Eq. 8 is borrowed from Kang et al. and applied to estimator outputs, not fitted as a power law. The measure is accuracy correlation, not loss. The extrapolation range is under 4x, and the result is the method's own performance. The data-selection experiment uses 5K/8K pilot budgets rather than 4K/8K; this does not affect the rows. No uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not measure held-out pretraining loss against language-model parameter count, tokens, or compute.
It projects validation accuracy, not language-model loss, from smaller to larger data budgets.
It does not optimize parameter and token allocation under a fixed compute budget.
It does not compare architecture details at a fixed parameter count.

The projection is tested only for validation accuracy in federated image-classification experiments. It does not test loss scaling or other listed regimes such as repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The paper predicts validation accuracy in federated training, but does not test downstream-task performance as a function of pretraining scale or pretraining loss.
It does not compare fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits across setup or fitting choices, or test whether curves depart from a single power law.

relation.reason: Uses neural scaling laws to project federated validation accuracy from smaller data budgets; does not test a catalog claim version.

tranche.reason: Equation (8) imports a scaling-based projection from reference [13]; the reported correlations evaluate the resulting performance-estimation method, without testing the power-law forms specified by the claim versions.

source_check.notes: The text reports approximately 0.88 correlation for both datasets without identifying the correlation statistic. These rows describe method performance and should not count as evidence testing scaling-law claim versions.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Federated image-classification accuracy on CIFAR10 and MNIST, projected from 4K and 8K trial budgets to 15K
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports high predicted-versus-true accuracy correlations (≈ 0.88) for both datasets; see r1 and r2. This supports the projection in this tested setting, but does not establish loss scaling or the other regimes named in V5.
